concepts.name: Background and Trigger Conditions of Kheda Satyagraha (1918)
key_dimensions: The dual crisis: crop failure due to floods/drought in 1917-18 combined with plague epidemic
Revenue remission rule: the colonial rule requiring remission if crop yield fell below one-fourth of normal
British administration's refusal to acknowledge the crop failure despite peasant petitions
Distinction from earlier peasant grievances — this was NOT about indigo or land tenure but about revenue assessment

concepts.name: Gandhi's Role and Entry into Gujarat Politics
key_dimensions: Kheda as Gandhi's first major peasant satyagraha on Indian soil (after Champaran in Bihar, 1917)
Difference in Gandhi's role: Champaran was investigative; Kheda was a direct revenue non-payment campaign
Gandhi's condition for joining: exhaustion of all constitutional/petitioning methods before civil disobedience
This being a turning point where Gandhi shifted from South African methods to Indian mass mobilization

concepts.name: Vallabhbhai Patel's Emergence as a Mass Leader
key_dimensions: Kheda Satyagraha as Patel's political debut alongside Gandhi — distinguishing it from Bardoli (1928) where Patel led independently
Patel's organizational role: touring villages, building peasant solidarity, and managing logistics
How Kheda shaped Patel's identity as 'Sardar' (the title came later at Bardoli but roots were in Kheda)
UPSC trap: Sardar title was conferred at Bardoli Satyagraha (1928), NOT Kheda

concepts.name: Core Demand and the Revenue Remission Principle
key_dimensions: The specific legal/administrative rule: remission applicable when produce was less than one-fourth (25%) of normal yield
Peasants' demand: suspension (not abolition) of revenue — a moderate, legally grounded demand
Difference between 'suspension' and 'remission' of revenue as strategic framing
British counter-argument: government surveys showed yield above the threshold — clash of data vs. ground reality

concepts.name: Methods and Tactics of the Satyagraha
key_dimensions: Pledge of non-payment: peasants who could afford to pay were also asked not to, as solidarity mechanism
No violence, no obstruction — purely passive resistance through non-payment
Use of mass meetings, pamphlets, and 'Young India' (newspaper) for propaganda
Gandhi's tactic of targeting wealthier peasants first to demonstrate sacrifice and inspire poorer ones

concepts.name: Indulal Yagnik and Shankarlal Banker's Contributions
key_dimensions: Indulal Yagnik's role in peasant mobilization and later divergence from Gandhian politics
Shankarlal Banker as a key organizer connecting urban Congress support to rural peasant movement
Significance: Kheda showed urban-rural Congress alliance — a model replicated later
UPSC angle: lesser-known leaders in Kheda vs. the dominant Gandhi-Patel narrative

concepts.name: British Administrative Response and Coercive Measures
key_dimensions: Attachment and auction of peasants' cattle, agricultural implements, and standing crops
Selective distraint: government targeted movable property rather than land to avoid fueling larger rebellion
Failure of coercion: peasants hid assets and neighbors refused to bid at auctions
How British coercion paradoxically strengthened peasant solidarity — a pattern seen in other satyagrahas

concepts.name: Resolution and Compromise of Kheda Satyagraha
key_dimensions: The unofficial settlement: government instructed revenue collectors to recover dues only from those who COULD pay, leaving the poor
Ambiguity of the outcome: Gandhi declared it a moral victory, but no formal written order was issued
Criticism of the settlement: some historians argue it was a face-saving compromise, not a clear peasant victory
UPSC trap: Kheda did NOT result in formal revenue remission legislation — contrast with Champaran's outcome (Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918)

concepts.name: Kheda vs. Champaran Satyagraha: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Champaran (1917): Against tinkathia system/indigo planters — agrarian contract dispute; led to formal legislation
Kheda (1918): Against government revenue demand — fiscal/administrative dispute; informal settlement
Champaran had a formal inquiry commission; Kheda relied purely on moral pressure
Both are Gandhi's early Indian satyagrahas but differ in adversary (private planters vs. colonial state directly)

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha and World War I Context
key_dimensions: The movement occurred while Gandhi was supporting British recruitment for WWI — an apparent contradiction
Gandhi's logic: supporting the war effort while simultaneously fighting unjust revenue policies
This dual stance was criticized — how can one be loyal and resistant simultaneously?
Post-war context: the Rowlatt Act (1919) transformed Gandhi from conditional supporter to full opponent

concepts.name: Role of Patidars (Patidar/Kanbi Community) in Kheda
key_dimensions: Patidars as the dominant peasant community in Kheda district — prosperous but affected by crop failure
Why Patidars led the movement: they had more to lose from distraint but also more capacity to sustain non-payment
Caste dynamics: movement was largely upper/middle peasant-led; poorer landless labor less involved
Long-term significance: Patidar political mobilization in Gujarat traces roots to Kheda and Bardoli

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha and the Evolution of Gandhian Mass Mobilization
key_dimensions: Kheda as a 'laboratory': tested methods of pledge-based non-compliance, village-level organization, and media use
Lessons carried forward to Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) and Civil Disobedience Movement (1930)
Shift from elite petition politics to mass civil disobedience — Kheda as a bridge
Difference: Kheda was local/regional; later movements were national in scope

concepts.name: Impact on Congress Organization in Gujarat
key_dimensions: Gujarat Sabha's role: the regional Congress body that first took up the Kheda issue before Gandhi's involvement
How Kheda strengthened the Gujarat Pradesh Congress Committee's organizational structure
Creation of a trained cadre of political workers — many went on to lead Bardoli (1928) and Salt March (1930)
UPSC angle: institutional continuity between Kheda, Bardoli, and Dandi — all Gujarat-based, all peasant-connected

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha and the Concept of 'Moral Victory' in Satyagraha Theory
key_dimensions: Gandhi's philosophical position: the goal of satyagraha is not just material outcome but transformation of adversary
Why Gandhi declared Kheda a 'moral victory' despite no formal concession
How this concept of moral victory was strategically important for sustaining future movements
Criticism: Does declaring ambiguous outcomes as victories erode credibility? Historians' debate

concepts.name: Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) as a Direct Descendant of Kheda
key_dimensions: Bardoli (1928) was also a revenue non-payment movement in Gujarat — same issue, same region, 10 years later
Key difference: Bardoli was led independently by Patel; Kheda was co-led with Gandhi
Bardoli had a clearer victory: the Simon Commission-era government conceded and appointed the Broomfield-Maxwell inquiry
UPSC trap: Sardar title was given to Patel at Bardoli (1928), not Kheda (1918) — frequently confused

concepts.name: Newspapers and Propaganda in Kheda Satyagraha
key_dimensions: Gandhi's use of 'Navajivan' (Gujarati) and 'Young India' (English) to publicize peasant grievances
Role of vernacular press in building local solidarity vs. English press for international/educated audience
Contrast with Champaran: Champaran relied more on inquiry-based reporting; Kheda used active campaigning
How controlled media messaging became a standard Gandhian tool — precedent set at Kheda

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha and Women's Participation
key_dimensions: Limited but notable women's participation — early precedent for later large-scale women's involvement in Civil Disobedience
Women's role: preventing cattle auctions, maintaining household solidarity during non-payment
Contrast with later movements: Salt Satyagraha (1930) and Quit India (1942) saw far greater women's mobilization
Why women's participation was constrained in 1918: social conservatism in rural Gujarat, Gandhi's own cautious approach at this stage

concepts.name: Limitations and Critiques of Kheda Satyagraha
key_dimensions: Class limitation: movement primarily represented land-owning peasants (Patidars), not landless laborers or artisans
Geographic limitation: confined to Kheda district — failed to spread to adjacent areas
Outcome ambiguity: no formal legislation or binding government order — contrasted unfavorably with Champaran
Historiographical debate: Sumit Sarkar and other historians question whether Kheda represented genuine mass mobilization or elite peasant interest protection

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha in the Context of 1917-1919 Nationalist Upsurge
key_dimensions: The cluster of events: Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918), Kheda (1918), Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919)
How this period marked Gandhi's rapid transformation from returning NRI to national leader in just 3-4 years
Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) and Kheda as simultaneous campaigns — Gandhi managing two satyagrahas at once
UPSC trap: Ahmedabad Mill Strike was about LABOR rights (wages); Kheda was about PEASANT rights (revenue) — same year, different issues, different classes

concepts.name: Legacy of Kheda Satyagraha in Post-Independence Revenue and Land Policies
key_dimensions: How Kheda established the precedent that crop failure = legitimate ground for revenue relief — later codified in Land Revenue Codes of independent India
Influence on the Zamindari Abolition movement's moral framing: peasants have rights against arbitrary state extraction
Patel's later role as Home Minister and his handling of Princely States — did Kheda experience inform his administrative style?
Academic angle: Kheda as a case study in 'rightful resistance' — peasants using state's own rules against it
